Bluetooth

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take you inside the sad world of Heroin addiction, and expose the horrific new trend called Bluetoothing

Unique Selling Point:
We have made contact with a group of homeless Heroin addicts who "Bluetooth" on a daily basis and are willing to show us and share their story.

Summary:
We start on the streets of Rosettenville in a derelict building. Our presenter is with a group of homeless drug addicts. They range in age from 14 to late 20's. We are about to witness the horrible reality of their everyday morning ritual - the sharing of heroin by injection in a process which has become known as Bluetooth/Bluetoothing. Where sharing a needle is nothing new for addicts, when bluetoothing they also share each other's blood. As they show us how they do it, our presenter asks them to talk us through it. The what, why and how etc. I will identify one of the users to tell us their story(one over 18years old). The user then becomes our central narrative - we spend a day in his life. From waking up on the streets to not being able to eat before his first hit, what they do during the day, how he earns money, to facing another bleak night on the streets. As his story unfolds we find out more of his back story. Where he came from, how he ended up on the streets, the dangers of the life etc. They face brutal attacks from gangs and criminals, rape etc. Police, often corrupt, are a constant threat. I want to shoot this very stylized, long lense on the grimy streets, sunset and another scary night approaching, the shadow people of the streets living in an umderworld while "normal life" happens all around them.

Interwoven into the central narrative, we bring in Margot Davids from JHB Child Welfare, Nelson Mederios from the Step Up Campaign etc to comment on the lives and circumstances that lead to addiction and the new Bluetoothing trend.

Press Release:


Bluetooth
They call it Bluetooth: injecting blood from a fellow drug addict to share the high. This practice is rife on South African streets and is riddled with serious health risks, but
users seem unperturbed. Carte Blanche heads into the dark world of heroin addiction to explore this growing phenomenon.

Script:


Bluetooth
10 May 2017

Voice
In March this year Carte Blanche exposed the rampant drug dealing happening on the streets of Rosettenville, Johannesburg.

Sound Up Hidden Camera
CB investigator: And what have you got?

Dealer: What do you want?

CB investigator: Cat.

Dealer: Cat? Ok R200.

CB investigator: R200 for how much?

Dealer: Nice bag.

Voice
Things got so bad that locals set fire to suspected drug dens and brothels. To really understand what motivates a community to such anger, you need to appreciate the devastation drugs bring to their lives and those of their loved ones.

Link Devi
When you think about Bluetooth, you immediately picture the sharing of information on a digital device, but when it comes to the grimy underworld of drugs, it has a whole other meaning.

Voice
The term Bluetooth refers to a disturbing trend amongst Heroin users. Practiced mostly by the poorest of the poor, addicts share their blood to get high.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Devi: You’ve only got money for one?
Peter: Ja
Devi: So what’s the plan, who’s going to spike, and who’s going to Bluetooth?
Peter: Ja I spike yesterday, he’s going to spike you see.
Devi: So yesterday was your turn, today is your turn?
Peter: Ja.




Voice
These two men, who we’ll call Peter and Richard, have agreed to talk to us on condition of anonymity. They are both severe heroin addicts. Their addictions have left them jobless and homeless on the streets of Rosettenville.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Devi: So you bought this morning?
Richard: Ja I bought this morning. Now I’m taking out my injection.
Devi: And how many times do you use one needle?
Richard: As long as it’s working.
Devi: Because the needles get blunt?
Richard: Ja
Devi: And it starts to hurt doesn’t it?”
Richard: Ja
Devi: But you don’t care?
Richard: I don’t feel it anymore.
Devi: Ok

Voice
Peter and Richard need to get their fix at least four times a day or suffer debilitating withdrawal symptoms. To earn money they beg at street corners. When the pickings are slim, they Bluetooth to get by.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Devi: So that was R30?
Richard: Ja this is R30. That’s what we are craving for.

Voice
Richard mixes the low-grade heroin with water before injecting himself. He’ll know he’s found a vein when his syringe fills with blood.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Richard: I’m looking for the vein now. You must get the right vein, because if you don’t get the right vein it’s going to hurt you this thing.
Peter: See he’s found a vein now you see?
Devi: Ok because now you’ve got the blood that’s spilling in.
Richard: Ja

Voice
Once he’s got his fix, he withdraws blood from the same vein back into the syringe to give to Peter. And then the Bluetooth moment arrives: Peter injects himself with Richard’s blood.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Devi: You found it?
Peter: Ja I found it.
Devi: How do you feel?
Peter: Ja it’s coming now you see.

Sound Up Thembi Ndubane
It’s amazing what people will think up and it’s amazing how they don’t realize what the dangers are. And they frankly don’t care about what the dangers are when they tell you.

Voice
Thembi Ndubane from the South African National Council on Alcoholism and Drug dependence says once addicts pass the point of no return, they will do anything for a fix.

Sound Up Thembi
They steal, you can only steal so much until the neighbours don’t want you anywhere near their things, they will sell their bodies, especially the females, until a certain point where nobody wants to buy anymore. But they have to get the high.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Peter: You see when you’re taking drugs you’re no more thinking about tomorrow you see. You just think for now you see, what you want you see. Because that thing for tomorrow, how can you think about tomorrow? You’re suffering now, you’re craving now you see.

Link Devi
While it may be tempting to forget drug addicts exist, the reality is they are a part of our society.

Voice
Professor Annie Hesselink is a criminologist from the Department of Criminology and Security Science at Unisa. She says there is a connection between substance abuse and society.

Sound Up Annie
It is a direct link to society and what is happening in society. The unemployment rate, the poverty. The emotional problems that individuals experience, the dysfunctional families, the lack of support systems. All of that can be traced to substance abuse.

Voice
Professor Hesselink says the Bluetooth phenomenon could easily transform from an act performed by the desperate to a trendy way of taking drugs. And the people most at risk? Our youth.


Sound Up Annie
Devi: But now when you’re talking young people, and when you start talking about bonding, this starts to get really serious now?
Annie: Drug use is learnt behavior, and peer pressure just enhances the whole process of using drugs. If they want a sense of belonging, if they want a substitute for the family, they will do anything to fit in and be part of that group. But of course it’s a matter of time, if not already there, where it is very cool to do so irrespective of the social class. Where it will have no boundaries regarding race, age gender or social strata.

Sound Up “Richard” & “Peter”
Devi: are a lot of people Bluetoothing?
Richard: Ja a lot of people are Bluetoothing.
Peter: Ja they are helping each other you see. Like what now we are doing you see. If I don’t have you see and it’s my friend this one you see, he won’t let me suffer of sickness you see. He will give me after he spike it you see. So at least I can go to hustle money.

Voice
The men are adamant that the practice is beneficial, a way of saving a friend from the severe pain of heroin withdrawal, seemingly oblivious to the possible dangers.

Link Devi
The concern is not just about HIV, the sharing of blood is a dangerous practice in itself.

Sound Up Thembi
Everybody has different types of blood. So I’ll be an A type somebody else will be a B type. So should that mix with something else that’s the wrong type of blood, then it causes an immune reaction, which could lead to death, which could be lethal.

Voice
Hepatitus, STD’s, the list is endless. But addicts like Richard and Peter simply don’t think that way.

Sound Up Richard and Peter
Devi: Are you not scared about sharing blood?
Peter: You see when you are sick, you don’t think about this guy is sick. He is helping you, how can you tell him he is sick, you see?

Voice
And for the thousands of addicts living on our streets, in our townships and suburbs, the chances of recovery, even if they could access the proper treatment facilities, are slim.
Sound Up Annie
What am I doing to my body has got nothing to do with it, the consequences attached to Bluetooth, they don’t care about it. They need that fix and they need it now, because they cannot go through withdrawal symptoms.

Sound Up Thembi
There is detox medication, but getting off Heroin is a massive, massive issue.

Sound Up Richard and Peter
Devi: Do you want to get out of this?
Richard: Ja, we do want to get out of it but eish…
Peter: It’s not easy when you are in the street to get out of it you see. Some guys they go to rehab you see, but when they come back they are still craving you see. Because this thing you can’t stop it you see.
